2011 textbook; texting features (acronyms, emoji) not corrupting but adding new register.
15th-18th century systematic change in long vowels; 'house' shifted from /hu:s/ to /haus/.
New experiences require new words; computing (download), pandemic (lockdown, social distancing).
First major English dictionary; 40,000 words; defined and prescribed usage; reduced spelling variation.
Underlying language influences invader's; British Celtic on Old English minimal; debated extent of influence.
Jean Piaget argued language reflects cognitive development; children acquire concepts before the words for them.
The understanding (developed around 8 months) that objects exist when out of sight — a prerequisite for naming absent things.
Mental structures for organising experience; assimilation extends a schema, accommodation revises it.
Piaget's first stage (0-2 years), in which language begins to label sensorimotor experience.
Piaget's term for early self-directed speech that he viewed as cognitively immature; Vygotsky disputed this, seeing it as social.
Chomsky's nativism stresses innate grammar; Piaget's constructivism stresses cognitive construction through interaction with the world.
Jerome Bruner proposed a Language Acquisition Support System — the structured caregiver interaction (peekaboo, joint attention) that scaffolds language.
Adult speech to children featuring exaggerated intonation, simplified vocabulary and frequent repetition — also called motherese.
Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development — the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with guidance.
Theory (Bruner, Vygotsky) that language emerges from meaningful interaction with caregivers, balancing innateness and learning.
Shared focus between caregiver and child on an object or event — a precursor to reference and naming.
Bruner's metaphor for the temporary support caregivers provide that is gradually withdrawn as the child becomes competent.
B. F. Skinner (Verbal Behavior 1957) argued language is learned through operant conditioning — imitation, reinforcement and correction.
Noam Chomsky proposed a Language Acquisition Device — an innate biological module enabling rapid grammar learning.
Chomsky's hypothesis that all human languages share a deep grammatical structure, accounting for the speed and uniformity of acquisition.
Chomsky's argument that the input children receive is too sparse to explain the grammar they produce, supporting innateness.
Errors like 'goed' or 'mouses' that show children apply rules, not imitate — a problem for pure behaviourism.
Eric Lenneberg (1967) proposed a developmental window (roughly pre-puberty) for full native acquisition.
18-24 months: combinations like 'more milk', 'daddy go' showing emergent syntax.
24-30 months: 3-4 word utterances missing function words (daddy go work), like an old telegram.
Martin Braine's analysis (1963) of two-word speech using high-frequency pivot words plus open class items.
Roger Brown's (1973) categories: agent-action, action-object, possessor-possession etc.
Mean Length of Utterance — average number of morphemes per utterance, an index of grammatical development.
Telegraphic speech drops articles, auxiliaries and inflections, keeping content words.
From around 30 months: function words reappear, morphology and complex syntax develop.
Jean Berko Gleason's 1958 test showed children could pluralise nonsense words (wugs), demonstrating internal rule knowledge.
Children master inflections in a predictable order — Brown's stages I-V.
Applying a regular pattern to an irregular form (goed, mouses), peaking after irregulars are first learned.
Coordination (and) appears first; subordination (because, when) follows.
Roger Brown's MLU-based progression from Stage I (1.75) to Stage V (4.0+), each tied to grammatical milestones.
0-6 months: melodic vowel-like sounds, exploring the vocal tract.
6-12 months: reduplicated (mama, dada) and variegated babble, narrowing toward the ambient language's phonology.
12-18 months: single words function as whole utterances (milk = I want milk).
The set of distinctive sounds in a language; babbling first explores broadly then narrows to ambient inventory.
Using a word for a wider class than its adult meaning (doggy for all four-legged animals).
Using a word for a narrower class (cup only for the child's own cup).
H. P. Grice (1975) — speakers cooperate in conversation, making contributions that fit the accepted purpose of the exchange.
Make your contribution as informative as required, no more, no less.
Do not say what you believe to be false or for which you lack evidence.
Be clear, brief, orderly; avoid obscurity and ambiguity.
Meaning inferred when a maxim is flouted — listeners reason about why the speaker broke it.
Conventional opening to talk: greeting + identification, especially in telephone calls (Schegloff).
Pre-closing tokens (well, anyway, okay) lead to terminal exchange (bye bye); closings are jointly negotiated.
Mechanisms for fixing trouble in talk — self-repair (I mean.), other-repair (Did you say Tuesday?).
Items like well, so, you know, right that organise discourse rather than carrying propositional content (Schiffrin 1987).
Listener feedback (mm, yeah, right) that signals attention without claiming the floor.
A linguistic device (sort of, kind of, maybe) that softens commitment to a proposition.
Sinclair & Coulthard (1975) Birmingham model: teacher Initiation, pupil Response, teacher Feedback.
A two-part exchange (question-answer, greeting-greeting, offer-acceptance) whose parts conventionally co-occur (Schegloff & Sacks).
Sacks, Schegloff & Jefferson (1974) — the orderly system by which speakers manage who talks next.
A point in an utterance where a turn change becomes legitimate.
Second parts of adjacency pairs that are unmarked (acceptance) versus marked, delayed and softened (refusal).
The third move in IRF — typically an evaluative 'Good' or 'Yes that's right' — signalling the teacher's authority.
A speaker's contribution between TRPs; the basic unit of conversational structure.
Mechanisms for assigning the next turn — current speaker selects next, or next self-selects.
The right to speak at a given moment; speakers compete for and yield the floor.
Two speakers talking simultaneously, often at a TRP (incidental) or in interruption (competitive).
Immediate uptake of the next turn with no gap or overlap — tight conversational fit.
Movement from one topic to another, often marked by discourse markers (anyway, by the way).
Power to introduce, develop and close topics — often asymmetric in institutional talk.
Halliday & Hasan (1976) — surface ties between sentences: reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, lexical cohesion.
Underlying sense and logical flow that allows a reader/listener to make a text 'add up' even without explicit cohesion.
Backward reference (Sarah. she.) tying later items to earlier mentions.
Set of related words across a discourse (doctor-patient-prescription) that sustains topical coherence.
Schegloff's structured initial exchange: summons, answer, identification, greeting.
Schegloff & Sacks's pre-closing tokens (well, anyway) leading to a terminal exchange.
Items like well, so, you know, right that organise discourse rather than carry propositional meaning (Schiffrin 1987).
Listener feedback (mm, yeah, right) signalling attention without claiming the floor.
A turn that sets up a later action: 'Are you busy?' often projects a request.
A sub-sequence between first and second pair-parts (Q-clarification-Q-A).

Robin Lakoff (Language and Woman's Place, 1975) argued women's language showed features of powerlessness — hedges, tags, super-polite forms.
Devices like 'sort of', 'I think' that soften assertion; Lakoff listed them as a female feature.
Phrases like 'isn't it?' appended to statements; Lakoff associated them with female speech and uncertainty.
Lakoff's term for evaluative items (lovely, divine) marked as feminine.
Use of more formal grammar than required, claimed by Lakoff as a marker of female speech.
Subsequent research (O'Barr & Atkins 1980) reframed Lakoff's features as 'powerless language', not female language.
Deborah Cameron (The Myth of Mars and Venus, 2007) showed alleged sex differences are exaggerated and often baseless.
Judith Butler's idea, adopted in linguistics — gender is produced by repeated stylised acts, including talk.
Eckert & McConnell-Ginet's framework, redirecting focus from male/female categories to local practice groups.
Kimberlé Crenshaw's concept — gender intersects with race, class, age and sexuality; language reflects multiple identities at once.
Linguistic features do not directly index gender but index stances and qualities (toughness, care) that are themselves gendered.
Awareness of gender stereotypes can shape speakers' own performance, reinforcing supposed differences.
Approach (Zimmerman & West 1975) that mixed-sex talk reflects male dominance, evidenced by male interruptions.
Recorded 31 conversations on a US campus; 96% of interruptions in mixed-sex pairs came from men.
Deborah Tannen's framework (You Just Don't Understand, 1990) — men and women belong to different sub-cultures and miscommunicate.
Status vs support, advice vs understanding, independence vs intimacy, orders vs proposals, conflict vs compromise, information vs feelings.
Tannen contrasts women's rapport talk (relational) with men's report talk (informational).
Critics (Cameron) argue the difference model recycles stereotypes and ignores power.
Cameron (2007) — the popular belief that men and women speak differently, used to sell self-help.
Reviews of many studies (Hyde 2005, Cameron 2007) find very small average gender differences in language behaviour.
Mehl et al. (2007) found women and men used roughly 16,000 words a day — no significant difference.
Awareness of stereotypes can shape behaviour, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Variation within men or within women dwarfs average differences between them.
Popular gender-difference books succeed because they confirm pre-existing beliefs.
Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) — identities intersect; gender combines with race, class, sexuality and age in language use.
Eckert & McConnell-Ginet (1992) — gender is produced within local groups, not by sex alone.
Research into how LGBTQ+ speakers construct identity through language; rejects fixed gay/straight binaries.
Linguistic features index stances and qualities (toughness, care) that become associated with gendered identities.
A speaker's positioning (epistemic, affective) within talk — central to performative gender.
Bundles of features used to project an identity in a context (Eckert third wave).
Robin Lakoff (1975) — women's language shows features of powerlessness.
Zimmerman & West (1975) — mixed-sex talk reflects male dominance through interruptions.
Deborah Tannen (1990) — men and women belong to different sub-cultures.
Butler / Cameron — gender is produced through talk; differences are exaggerated.
O'Barr & Atkins (1980) — Lakoff's features index status, not sex.
Hybrid of speech and writing; openings, sign-offs and politeness vary by status and familiarity.
Genre with chairs allocating turns, agendas constraining topic and minutes formalising outcomes.
Brief written directive with To/From/Subject headers and clear action points.
Softening of FTAs with hedges, conditionals and politeness markers ('Could I ask.').
Brand-consistent register imposed by style guides — friendly but authoritative.
Workplace communication combines text, images, links and emoji — meaning across modes.
Asymmetric talk featuring history-taking, diagnosis and treatment recommendations; doctors typically control topic.
Highly constrained — barristers ask, witnesses answer; closed and tag questions dominate cross-examination.
Sinclair & Coulthard's teacher Initiation, pupil Response, teacher Feedback structure.
Open questions invite narrative; closed and tag questions constrain — used by powerful participants to control.
Goffman's term — a speaker realigns within talk (e.g. doctor switches from clinician to confidant).
Tailoring talk to the specific audience — central to expert-lay communication.
Drew & Heritage (1992) — workplace interactions characterised by goal-orientation, asymmetry and special inferential frameworks.
Workplace talk is organised around institutional purposes (treatment, transaction, instruction).
One participant typically controls topic, turns and evaluation (doctor vs patient, manager vs subordinate).
Specialist vocabulary shared by an occupational group; can index expertise but also exclude outsiders.
Talk between specialists and non-specialists, requiring accommodation and translation of jargon.
Speakers performing professional roles through register, lexis and discourse strategies.
Any utterance (request, refusal, criticism) that threatens speaker or hearer face, requiring mitigation.
Direct expression of an FTA without redress (Sit down), reserved for emergencies or marked status difference.
Strategy emphasising solidarity with the hearer (We're all in this together) to soften an imposition.
Strategy minimising imposition on autonomy (I hate to ask, but.), deferential and indirect.
Interactions where managerial participants control turn allocation, topic and evaluative feedback (Drew & Heritage 1992).
Erving Goffman (1981) described shifts in speaker alignment that recalibrate institutional roles within talk.
Power that operates through persuasion, ideology and rhetoric rather than overt force.
A rhetorical structure of three parallel elements (education, education, education) used to lend rhythm and authority.
Verbs (must, should, will) that encode authority and certainty within persuasive texts.
Speakers deploy inclusive 'we' to align with audiences and exclusive 'they' to construct out-groups.
An implicit assumption embedded in an utterance (When did you stop wasting taxpayers' money?) that smuggles in a claim.
Gramsci's concept (used by Fairclough) for power maintained by manufactured consent rather than coercion.
Power held by institutions (law, education, government) and enacted through language that demands compliance.
Critical Discourse Analysis (Norman Fairclough, 1989) examining how language reproduces social power and ideology through three levels: text, discursive practice and social practice.
Brown and Levinson (1987) describe positive face (need to be liked) and negative face (need for autonomy); face-threatening acts (FTAs) require politeness strategies.
Interactions where one participant holds greater status, controlling turn-taking, topic and lexis (e.g. courtroom, classroom).
Fairclough's term for the way mass media simulates one-to-one intimacy with audiences using inclusive pronouns and direct address.
A newly coined word or expression (selfie, doomscroll, ick).
Abbreviation pronounced letter by letter (LOL, BTW, OMG), proliferating in digital discourse.
David Crystal argues internet English is a new variety, neither speech nor writing but a third medium, and language is healthier than ever.
Halliday's view (SFL) that language changes to meet the communicative needs of its users.
Chen's S-curve describes how innovations spread slowly at first, accelerate, then plateau.
Charles Hockett's theory that small random changes accumulate without overall direction.
Change observed across time, contrasted with synchronic snapshots of a single moment.
A systematic change in long vowel pronunciation in English roughly 1400-1700, reshaping the phonology.
Adoption of words from other languages: French (after 1066), Latin (Renaissance), global English borrowings.
The process by which lexical items become grammatical markers (Old English 'gan' to modern 'going to' future).
Semantic shift where a word acquires more positive connotations (knight: boy to noble warrior).
Semantic shift where a word acquires more negative connotations (silly: blessed to foolish).
Aitchison's metaphor for the prescriptivist view that English was once perfect and is now decaying — a view she rejects.
Aitchison's metaphor for the idea that bad usage spreads through contact, like a virus; she argues speakers adopt forms they find useful.
Aitchison's metaphor for the view that change is caused by laziness, like a damp spoon left in sugar; she dismisses it as inaccurate.
Change in word meaning: amelioration, pejoration, broadening, narrowing.
The view that language should follow fixed rules; associated with Jonathan Swift's 1712 proposal for an English Academy.
The view that linguists describe how language is used without judging usage; associated with David Crystal.
Jean Aitchison's damp spoon, crumbling castle and infectious disease — three prescriptivist views she rejected.
Michael Halliday's Systemic Functional Linguistics treats language as a meaning-making resource with three metafunctions.
Language used to represent experience (transitivity, processes, participants).
Language used to enact social relationships (mood, modality).
Language used to organise discourse (theme, cohesion).
Halliday's view that language changes when speakers need to mean new things — driving lexical and grammatical innovation.
David Crystal's view that linguistics describes how language is used; change is healthy and normal.
The view that language should conform to fixed rules — rejected by mainstream linguistics but persistent in public debate.
Differences across regions, classes, ages and contexts — variation is the raw material of change.
Historical processes (Haugen's stages) by which one dialect becomes the standard.
Younger speakers leading change tend to consolidate the new form into the standard over time.
Crystal's term for the conventions of computer-mediated communication, a new third medium.
Johannes Schmidt's 1872 model — change radiates outward from an innovation centre, weakening with distance.
Chen's S-curve plots adoption against time: slow start, rapid uptake, plateau.
William Wang's theory — phonological change spreads word by word through the lexicon, not all at once.
Charles Hockett's view — small accidental variations accumulate into systematic change without overall purpose.
Change attributed to influence of a previous or contact language (Celtic on English, Norman on Middle English).
Halliday — change happens because speakers need to express new meanings.

How airflow is shaped: plosive (p,b), fricative (f,v), nasal (m,n), affricate (ch,j), approximant (w,y).
Smallest meaningful unit of sound; English has around 44 phonemes; minimal pairs (pat/bat) distinguish them.
Where sound is made: bilabial (m), labiodental (f), alveolar (t), velar (k), glottal (h).
Rhythm, stress and intonation patterns; pitch movement (rising for questions); supports meaning beyond words.
Vocal cord vibration distinguishes voiced (b,d,g,v,z) from voiceless (p,t,k,f,s) pairs.
William Labov's 1966 study of rhotic /r/ in Saks, Macy's and S. Klein, showing higher-prestige stores produced more post-vocalic /r/.
Public, conscious value attached to standard or high-status forms; aspirational speakers shift toward them.
Hidden value of non-standard forms within in-groups, signalling solidarity (Trudgill 1974 Norwich).
Peter Trudgill (1974) found working-class men over-reported non-standard forms, demonstrating covert prestige.
A linguistic feature that varies across speakers (post-vocalic /r/, /h/-dropping, glottal stop).
Systematic patterning of variants by social class, age, gender or context.
A feature whose realisation correlates with social factors — Labov's central analytic unit.
Labov's 1963 study of /aɪ/ and /aʊ/ on the Massachusetts island; centralisation marked island identity against summer tourists.
A youth variety described by Cheshire, Kerswill, Fox and Torgersen (2011) in multi-ethnic London, with features from Jamaican, South Asian and Cockney sources.
Reduction of distinctive regional features under mobility, mass media and contact (Kerswill).
The formation of a new variety from contact between dialects (e.g. Milton Keynes new town speech).
A variety associated with an ethnic group, often within a wider linguistic community.
Cheshire et al. found such groups in London accelerated MLE features regardless of individual ethnicity.
A group united by shared activity and practice (Eckert & McConnell-Ginet 1992) — more dynamic than fixed social class.
Penelope Eckert's Detroit high-school ethnography showed identity groups (jocks/burnouts) drove vowel variation more than parental class.
Approach (Eckert 2012) focused on style, identity construction and indexicality rather than fixed correlations.
The way linguistic features point to (index) social identities and stances.
Speakers adjusting features by context, audience or stance — central to Labov's attention-to-speech model.
Howard Giles (1973) — speakers converge toward or diverge from interlocutors to manage social distance.
